DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
The proposal's direction may well be right, since the hotel is priced below its competitive set and has strong summer demand. But the main piece of evidence on price sensitivity is confounded by the season, the revenue figure uses the wrong room count and is a ceiling rather than a floor, and the two-night minimum conflicts with the hotel's own wedding business.

## What checks out

- **The occupancy figures are consistent.** The monthly figures in Table 1 average 79.2%, matching the stated 79%.
- **The competitor gap is right.** Against competitor rates of £165–£180, £145 is £20–£35 below.
- **The trigger is reasonable.** At £165, the hotel earns the same revenue per available room as today at about 69% occupancy. So the trigger at five points below 2025 fires well before the increase starts losing money.

## 1. The room count is wrong in the revenue calculation

Section 2 says Harbourside has **112 rooms**, but section 5 uses **124**.

- With 124 rooms: 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ **£204,000**
- With 112 rooms: 112 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ **£184,000**

The headline figure is overstated by about £20,000 before any other adjustment.

## 2. The "natural experiment" is a seasonal effect

The key evidence is that occupancy rose from 81% in June to 89% in July after the £10 increase. But the document itself explains why July is strong: "the harbour festival and the school summer holidays." July and August are the peak months every year. A rise from June to July is what you'd expect at any price, so the comparison says nothing about price sensitivity.

There's a second problem. The increase took effect in the last week of June, and much of July's business would already have been booked at £135 by then.

A meaningful test would compare the months after the increase with the same months in 2024, for example July–December 2025 against July–December 2024. It would also be worth checking whether booking pace slowed after the change.

The 8.4 value-for-money score has a similar weakness. It was measured while Harbourside was the cheapest hotel in its set, so a high value score is partly a result of that low price. It doesn't show how guests would rate value at £165.

## 3. £204,000 is a ceiling, not a floor

Several factors push the real figure down from the headline:

- **Not every occupied room pays BAR.** Section 6 says corporate and contracted group rates will be honoured, and 38% of Saturday bookings are wedding blocks. Applying £20 to every occupied room overstates the gain, possibly by a lot.
- **Bookings already on the books.** Stays from 1 June that are already booked at £145 won't pay the new rate, so the first year collects less than a full year's uplift.
- **Assuming occupancy holds is not prudent.** Section 5 calls flat occupancy "prudent," but raising the rate by 14% and expecting no loss of volume is optimistic. A cautious estimate would allow for some loss, for example showing results at −2, −5 and −8 points.
- **The minimum stay can lose business as well as gain it.** Guests who want only Saturday night may book a competitor instead. So the unquantified two-night effect could be negative as well as positive.

## 4. The two-night minimum conflicts with the wedding business

Section 4 makes two statements that pull against each other:

- The minimum stay will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays.
- Wedding guests, who make up **38% of Saturday bookings**, typically arrive on Saturday and leave on Sunday morning.

Wedding guests are the clearest case of a one-night Saturday stay and are unlikely to stay a second night. That leaves two possibilities:

- **The minimum applies to wedding guests.** The hotel risks losing a large, reliable block to competitors, and possibly souring the relationship with Quayside Hall.
- **Wedding blocks are exempt as groups.** The minimum then applies to only about 62% of Saturday demand. The proposal should say this and estimate the effect on that basis.

The minimum also applies to every Saturday of the year, but the case for it rests on the 31 sold-out Saturdays. In January, when weekend occupancy is 62%, turning away a one-night Saturday booking means an empty room. Most hotels apply minimum stays only on high-demand dates.

## 5. Smaller points

- **The monitoring is reactive.** A monthly occupancy trigger is reasonable, but weekly pick-up against the same weeks in 2025 is the earlier warning. The proposal should say what happens if pick-up falls behind, for example a review after three consecutive weeks below pace.
- **"Bring into line" versus "low risk":** at £165 the hotel will be level with the cheapest competitor, not below it. That's reasonable, but the cushion of being the value option disappears, so the risk is higher than in the 2025 increase.

## Suggested changes before approval

1. Correct the room count and re-base the estimate on BAR-paying rooms only. Exclude corporate, contracted group and wedding rooms, and allow for business already on the books.
2. Replace the June-to-July comparison with a year-on-year comparison for the months after the 2025 increase.
3. Show the revenue at several occupancy outcomes, alongside the break-even of about 69%.
4. Decide how wedding blocks are treated, and limit the two-night minimum to high-demand Saturdays, for example dates forecast above 90%, instead of all year.
5. Add a pick-up trigger alongside the monthly occupancy trigger.

With these changes, the proposal would be a well-evidenced case for a rate rise that looks justified. As written, the evidence is weaker and the upside smaller than it claims.
